title: An exact information theory of generalization phase transitions in Bayesian diffusion models
authors: Henry Hunt, Mason Kamb, Surya Ganguli
abstract: How diffusion models circumvent the curse of dimensionality to learn complex distributions over high dimensional spaces from a finite training set, instead of memorizing it, remains a fundamental mystery. To address this, we introduce analytically tractable Bayesian information restricted diffusion (BIRD) models, in which each pixel observes restricted information about noisy data. A BIRD model time-reverses diffusion by inferring which past training sample produced its current restricted observation using the Bayesian posterior. This model class generalizes existing analytical diffusion models that use spatially local information restriction. We show that spatially local BIRD models closely approximate trained diffusion models \textit{early in training}, across different architectures such as UNets and DiTs. Under minimal assumptions on the data distribution, we identify an information-theoretic phase boundary between memorization and generalization in the joint space of amount of training data, time in the reverse generative process, and amount of information restriction: a BIRD model memorizes when the mutual information between its restricted noisy observations and the training data exceeds the log number of training points, and it generalizes otherwise. Experiments across a range of datasets confirm our theoretically predicted location for the transition. We find that generation proceeds near the edge of memorization: both spatially local BIRD models and early-training diffusion models track the memorization-generalization phase boundary by increasingly restricting information over time. Overall, our results reveal a fundamental role for information restriction in generative AI to circumvent the curse of dimensionality.
summary: This paper develops the Bayesian Information Restricted Diffusion (BIRD) model to theoretically understand how generative AI generalizes from limited data. It establishes a precise information-theoretic boundary separating memorization from true generalization based on mutual information. The findings reveal that successful generation requires operating precisely at this phase transition edge, providing fundamental insights into deep learning's capacity limits.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental mystery of how diffusion models generalize from finite data without memorizing the training set in high-dimensional spaces.
main_result: It identifies an information-theoretic phase boundary determining when a model transitions between memorization and generalization, showing that optimal generation occurs near this boundary.
method: The authors introduce Bayesian Information Restricted Diffusion (BIRD) models and derive theoretical criteria based on mutual information to characterize the transition point.
model_or_system: The core system is the BIRD model, which restricts pixel observations ($C_{x,t}$) during diffusion reversal. The analysis compares this analytical framework against empirical training of standard neural architectures like UNets and DiTs.
key_observables: Mutual Information ($	ext{MI}$), $r^2$ correlation coefficient, critical patch scale ($L_c(t)$).
important_parameters: Amount of training data, time/noise level in the reverse process ($t$), and amount of information restriction (patch size $L$).
main_assumptions: The theoretical criterion relies on mild assumptions about the underlying data distribution; local approximations are used to model complex architectures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing the transition boundary between memorization and generalization, and show quantitative comparisons of analytical models against early-training results for various datasets.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the problem (generalization mystery) to introducing the BIRD model framework. It then develops the information-theoretic criterion for the phase transition, validates this theory by comparing it to empirical training data across multiple architectures, and concludes by showing that optimal generation tracks this theoretical boundary.
why_interesting: The work provides a rigorous, information-theoretic lens (related to complexity measures used in statistical physics) to analyze generalization failure modes in modern deep learning models, connecting concepts of phase transitions to AI performance.

(a) A depiction of the Bayesian guessing game performed by a pixel as it assigns posterior probabilities to training set images. The forward process starts with a training image of a cat, adds noise to it, then the pixel observes a local patch (e.g. the eye). Based on this restricted observation, the pixel must guess whether this noisy patch was generated from the truck or the cat. The pixel memorizes if the posterior con- centrates on the cat. Here UNets and DiTs are trained on disjoint dataset subsets D1 and D2, but produce nearly identical images when fed the same noise input. These images are both similar to the corresponding BIRD model outputs. Many more such samples are shown in App. H.2 in figs. 7-11, along with details of the experiment and training procedure in App. H.

Figure 3: Comparison of theory and experiment for the memorization-generalization phase tran- sition. Experimental curves plot numerical estimates of the average entropy deficit (ln |D| − S[P(φ|ϕΩ)]) in a spatially local BIRD model with a patch size 5 × 5. σ2 t is the noise strength. Theory curves plot mutual information or its Gaussian upper bounds. As noise σ2 t decreases, the theoretically derived mutual information curves rise in the generalizing phase then saturate to ln |D| in the memorizing phase.
